We have better maps of Mars than of our own seafloor. That fact deserves a moment of sitting with. The red planet, barren and airless, has been surveyed down to its craters by orbiting spacecraft with nothing to obstruct their view. Meanwhile, beneath five kilometers of ocean lies terrain we've seen in less detail than the surface of the Moon—because water, paradoxically, is harder to see through than vacuum. Radar bounces off it. Light gives out after a few hundred meters.

So most of Earth is a rumor. We know the mid-ocean ridges exist, winding chains of mountains longer than any range on land, where the planet exhales new crust. We know hydrothermal vents host ecosystems that run on chemistry rather than sunlight—tubeworms like pale candles, shrimp crowding around chimneys of superheated water. But for every canyon we've lowered a camera into, thousands remain unvisited. Creatures drift up in nets with translucent skin and eyes like question marks, and no one knows what they look like alive.

I find this oddly comforting. In an age when every corner of the map seems claimed, photographed, and reviewed, the largest habitat on Earth remains essentially unlit, unmapped, unmet. Somewhere below the reach of sunlight there are animals we will never name, singing and flashing color at each other in the dark, going about lives that have nothing to do with us. The world keeps a few secrets, and I hope it keeps them a long time.
